newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan rightist vows to erect house on disputed isle.
newsitem.headline: Japan rightist vows to erect house on disputed isle.

text.p: Japanese ultra-nationalists who built a lighthouse that caused a row over the East China Sea islands claimed by Japan, China and Taiwan said on Monday they aimed to build an additional house there.
"We want to build a house there sometime next year," said a senior official of the Japan Youth Federation.
"We will probably erect one about 30 metres (yards) away from our lighthouse," the official, who declined to be further identified, told Reuters in an interview.
Last July, the same rightist group built a makeshift lighthouse on one of the islands, sparking sharp reactions from China and Taiwan and anti-Japan protests in Hong Kong.
Last month, Japan's coast guard prevented Taiwanese and Hong Kong activists from landing on the islands, called the Senkakus in Japanese and Diaoyus in Chinese.
But Japan's coast guard said they failed to "persuade" the Japanese Youth Federation members from making a landing on the islands last Wednesday.
Beijing says China has owned the islets since ancient times. Tokyo says the islands have been Japanese since 1895.
Several of the right-wing group's members would take up residence at the house for regular maintenance work on the lighthouse, the group official said.
"Next year is special to us because it will be 20 years since we first erected a lighthouse there," he said.
In a separate interview with Reuters, federation leader Toyohisa Eto said that an alternative plan to building a house was to tow a "floating pier" to waters near the island.
Eto said the group was motivated by safety concerns.
"We built the lighthouse to ensure safety of ships and tankers in the East China Sea. That's crucial to Japan which relies on crude oil from the Middle East," Eto said.
"We are relieved that all the protesters (from Taiwan and Hong Kong) were evicted from Japan's territorial waters," he added.
Touching on a separate island dispute with South Korea, Eto accused the Japanese government of what he described as "weak-knee diplomacy" towards Seoul.
"We still have this dispute with South Korea because of the Japanese government's weak-knee diplomacy," he said.
He said Tokyo should have resolved the dispute over the small Sea of Japan islet known as Tokto in Korea and Takeshima in Japan when the two countries signed a peace treaty in 1965.
South Korea has built buildings and effectively controls the island, which it says was illegally transferred to Japan in the early 20th century. Japan says its claim dates back to 1905.
The long-dormant disputes were rekindled last year when East Asian countries declared 200-nautical-mile exclusion zones around their coasts based on the new U.N. Convention on the Law of the Sea.
Both island groups are located in rich fishing grounds and may also hold other untapped natural resources, such as oil.
